A single reading taken by your doctor at the clinic is just a snapshot of what's going on in your body at that moment. Monitoring your blood pressure at home gives you a better picture of the bigger picture by providing you with the readings you take on ordinary days when you're not under the stress of being at the clinic.
How Often Should You Measure Your Blood Pressure?
If you've been diagnosed with high blood pressure or your doctor has asked you to take readings, take readings for about seven days before you're due for an appointment or after you've changed your medication.
Take readings twice a day, in the morning and in the evening, and take two readings each time, one minute apart. Many guidelines say that you should discard the results from the first day and average the rest. Once your blood pressure is well controlled, you can cut back to a few times a week or even to a one-week round every month or so, but make sure your clinician agrees. If you don't have a diagnosis but you're concerned about your blood pressure, then occasional checks can help, especially if you're over 40 or have risk factors for high blood pressure such as family history, diabetes, excess weight, or kidney disease.
A reasonable frequency is to take a week of readings every few months or whenever a reading taken at the clinic is high. But don't assume that more is always better. Constant checking can fuel anxiety and make you overreact to normal fluctuations in your blood pressure. Blood pressure naturally rises and falls throughout the day, and the patterns are more important than individual readings.
When During the Day?
Consistency is key. Take your readings at the same times each day so that you can compare the results. For a morning reading, take it within an hour of waking, after you've been to the bathroom, before you've eaten, had coffee, done exercise, or taken your blood pressure medication. Blood pressure tends to surge in the morning, and this surge is linked to cardiovascular events, making these readings especially valuable. Don't measure your blood pressure after caffeine, smoking, exercise, or drinking alcohol, and wait at least 30 minutes before you measure again.
The Right Technique
Even a good blood pressure device can mislead you if you don't set it up correctly. Small errors in technique can result in blood pressure readings that are 10 points or more higher or lower than they should be. Some of the most overlooked errors include the following:
  • Cuff size: One of the most overlooked errors in measuring blood pressure is using a cuff that's the wrong size. A cuff that's too small will give a reading that's too high, and one that's too large can give a reading that's too low. Check the cuff size to make sure you're using the right size for you. Measure the middle of your upper arm and compare it to the size range in the cuff or manual. A standard cuff is usually included with a blood pressure monitor, but other sizes are sold separately.
  • Cuff placement: Place the cuff on your bare skin, not over your clothing, and roll up your sleeve if it's not loose enough, but avoid the tourniquet effect. If you put the cuff on your arm above or below the heart level, you'll get a falsely high or falsely low reading, respectively. Crossing your legs or dangling your feet can noticeably raise your blood pressure.
  • Resting first: Before you take a reading, sit quietly for at least five minutes. Don't talk, scroll through your phone, or engage in any stressful activity, and make sure your bladder is empty (a full bladder can raise your blood pressure reading).
  • Validated upper-arm monitor: An automatic blood pressure monitor that measures your blood pressure in your upper arm is generally more accurate than those that measure your blood pressure in your wrist or on your finger. Choose a clinically validated monitor, and consider bringing it to your appointment to compare to the clinic equipment.
  • Same arm each time: It's best to take your readings on the same arm, and ideally the arm that tends to give the higher reading, as your doctor may advise.
Making Sense of the Numbers
If your home average blood pressure is 130/80 or higher, this is an elevated blood pressure that's high enough to discuss with your doctor. Blood pressure targets vary by individual, so don't try to diagnose or adjust your medication yourself. Bring your log to your appointment so that your clinician can see the full pattern.
It's also important to get urgent attention if your blood pressure is 180/120 or higher, especially if you have symptoms such as chest pain, shortness of breath, severe headache, changes in vision, weakness, or difficulty speaking. And if you get a very high blood pressure reading without any symptoms, rest for five minutes and then remeasure. If it's still that high, contact your doctor promptly.

In contract law, parties enter into agreements that create their own obligations. In tort law, however, the law imposes a duty. Tort law requires people to act reasonably, not to deliberately harm others, and not to make false statements that damage someone’s reputation. When it comes to business, the difference between tort and contract law is important because it means that you can be exposed to liability even if you don’t sign a document. For example, a delivery driver may crash into someone, a business may publish a false accusation on its website, or a manufacturer’s product may injure a bystander.
The distinction between intentional and unintentional torts matters because intentional wrongdoing can result in the imposition of punitive damages. Insurance policies often exclude intentional acts and cover only negligence. Intentional torts require a deliberate act that results in harm. In these cases, it is sufficient that the person intend the act itself and not the full extent of the damage. Negligence, on the other hand, has four elements that must be proven: the duty of care, breach of that duty, causation, and damages.
Businesses are exposed to liability in the area of cyber torts. They may commit cyber torts as perpetrators (although this is a rare occurrence), but they are more likely to be exposed to liability as custodians of sensitive data. Businesses that fail to protect sensitive data with reasonable safeguards can be subject to liability in the form of negligence claims after a breach as well as regulatory enforcement and statutory penalties.

Is Texas done studying why mothers die?
The answer is yes, but the task force has only just scratched the surface. It’s not enough, and the task force, which diagnoses, can’t cure. That’s the Legislature’s job.
The task force’s work is on the agenda for the special session. Lawmakers should pass it quickly.
The task force brings together physicians, nurses, epidemiologists and public health experts to review maternal deaths case by case. It’s revealed, for instance, that a death labeled “cardiac arrest” followed weeks of untreated hypertension. Another death was caused by an overdose after the mother lost access to treatment.
Later reviews of the task force’s findings revealed data and reporting errors, including how pregnancy is recorded on death certificates, that inflated some of the figures. Data problems don’t erase the reality that mothers are still dying of causes that are often preventable. And the deaths fall hardest on the same women repeatedly.
The task force’s findings can’t be quickly rebuilt if there are lapses. Letting them expire in the middle of a crisis, while the data is being corrected, is indefensible.
Who is dying and why
An early analysis of the task force’s work found that Black women in Texas account for about one in nine births but nearly three in ten maternal deaths. Income and education don’t explain away the gap. Researchers pointed to a lack of access to care, untreated chronic conditions like hypertension before pregnancy, and how patients are heard or not when they report symptoms.
Texas Medicaid covers about half of births. For many low-income mothers, Medicaid coverage for pregnancy ends roughly 60 days after delivery. The task force said a large share of maternal deaths occur after that coverage window closes, including deaths caused by cardiac conditions, overdoses and suicide.
Overdose is one of the leading causes of maternal death in Texas, often well after delivery. Women who are stable during pregnancy can lose access to substance use treatment and mental health care after their baby arrives.
Texas didn’t expand Medicaid. Parent income limits are among the strictest in the country. Mothers go from coverage to none just as the risks of pregnancy turn deadly.
Studying is not the same as solving
Extending postpartum coverage is not an easy vote for lawmakers to cast. They should do it.
The harder test is acting on what the task force says. Funding study but not preventive care is choosing to document a tragedy rather than end it.

In my thought experiment about the writings attributed to Khalil Gibran, the language is reduced to seven words. My rule is not that these words are the most beautiful or useful, but rather the words that cannot be replaced by anything else. I trust the bodies and actions, but they only hint at some things, and I keep those words.
What the Seven Words Teach
We all live in the space between people, in the spaces of trust and risk and promise, where pointing is not enough.
Love
I cannot always tell what actions are love and what actions are duty or habit or guilt. But when I say the word I remove the ambiguity. It is a risk because the word is named and I cannot hide behind the implication. But I keep the word because it makes the actions mean something.
Forgive
Apologies can be mimed with a bowed head. Forgiveness can’t be performed in silence because silence is what resentment looks like. Sometimes the wrongdoer waits years for a releasing sentence and the speaker is released too. A hug might mean anything. “I forgive you” means one thing.
Friend
This is a word of promotion. The acquaintances become friends when one says “you’re my friend.” The naming changes the relationship. When I was introduced to someone as “my friend” for the first time I felt the largeness of it, because no action could confer that status. It had to be said.
Believe / Trust
I have been given both of these things in low moments and a quiet “I believe in you” has held longer than any act of rescue.
Always
This is a needed word because actions happen only in the present. A kind gesture today says nothing about tomorrow. Only a word reaches forward. “This is not just for now.” It may not always be true, but the willingness to say and mean it is deeply human.

The 93% Body Language Myth: Mehrabian
A lot of people are surprised to hear that the actual measure was quite narrow. What Mehrabian was trying to find out was how people judge feelings and attitudes when the words you say clash with your tone of voice or expression. He never said that 93% of all meaning is outside language – and you can’t learn a tax law lecture by just watching someone’s hands. When your words and body language disagree, people believe the body.
Why does the body get the final vote?
We’re communicating on two channels at once. The verbal channel carries the content – the facts, requests and opinions – and the nonverbal channel carries the relationship. A sincere apology while you scroll on your phone lands as an insult. Tough feedback with steady, open attention can land as care.
The governing principle is to use body language to express what is true, not manufacture what isn’t. People spot incongruence – a smile that doesn’t reach your eyes, or eye contact that feels like a stare-down. They feel it even when they can’t name it, and trust erodes.
Wanting to listen but having posture that says “I’m in a hurry” – adjusting that is not manipulation, it’s letting your intention through. But pretending interest when you have none? No posture will save you, and shouldn’t.
De-escalating tension: lower your physical intensity, sit if they sit, angle to the side instead of face-to-face, drop your shoulders. Standing over someone you’re in disagreement with reads as dominance even if it’s not intended.
In emotional or vulnerable moments, side-by-side (walking or driving) can ease hard topics by reducing eye contact. Looking away can be kind.
Pointing, chopping, finger-jabbing escalate conflict fast. If you’re aiming for resolution, soften those gestures.
Confidence or authority: upright, balanced weight, unhurried movement. Confidence is stillness, not taking up space. No fidgeting or retreating.
You lean in and they lean back. Give them some space. They mirror a relaxed posture – connection is growing.
In our cultural differences, norms vary widely. A sustained gaze can read as disrespect.
Read the room. Including yourself. They lean back when you lean in? Give them some space. They mirror a relaxed posture? Connection is growing.
Also notice your own body. Clenching your jaw before a meeting or crossing your arms when a certain topic comes up are signals you should heed. Sometimes an honest adjustment is to your understanding of how you feel, not your posture.

The key takeaway is that while GDP is an excellent measure of total market output, it is a poor stand-alone measure of well-being. Real GDP per capita is preferred when comparing living standards, but should be interpreted with caution.
If country A has four times the total output of country B, then on a per person basis A has a GDP of $10,000 while B has a GDP of $50,000. Thus, on average, a person in country B has far more goods and services than a person in country A.
If real GDP grows by 3 percent but the population grows by 4 percent, then output per person falls. Given this, we would expect that on average living standards are declining.
In many cases, PPP adjustments are used to account for price-level differences across countries.
A country with identical GDP per capita could still have very different living conditions if the income distribution is very broad (i.e., there are large differences between the highest and lowest incomes) or concentrated (i.e., there is not a lot of difference between the highest and lowest incomes).
For example, if the top 1 percent of households in a country earn half of all income, then the per capita income may look healthy, but the typical household in that country may struggle. Furthermore, just because GDP is rising does not mean that everyone is experiencing gains; GDP growth can concentrate among high earners while median incomes remain stagnant.
Non-market production is also excluded, such as unpaid housework, childcare, and volunteer work. Although this activity has real value, it does not take place through a market transaction. The size of the shadow economy varies widely across countries. In some developing countries, informal economic activity may represent a large share of output, so official GDP figures can substantially understate economic activity and make cross-country comparisons less accurate.
When a polluting factory is built, this activity increases GDP. However, the lost water quality and associated health costs are not subtracted. Similarly, if a disaster occurs and cleanup increases GDP because repair/remediation spending is counted as production, then this is also an example of GDP not accurately reflecting well-being. The link between this issue and negative externalities is that costs that impact third parties are not captured in market prices. Because GDP is built from market transactions, these negative externalities are missed. This means that a country can post strong economic growth while degrading its natural capital that future generations will need.

Wrong Form and Dose Can Push Iodine High Enough to Disrupt the Thyroid It's Marketed to Help
Seaweed supplements can be sold as dried snacks, powdered "sea greens," kelp tablets, or capsules, and they're sometimes marketed as ways to support the thyroid, detox the body, and achieve metabolic balance.
Iodine is an essential nutrient our bodies need in tiny amounts: adults about 150 micrograms (µg) per day, pregnant women about 220 µg, and breastfeeding women about 290 µg. Our upper limits for iodine are modest, too: in the United States, adults can safely ingest up to 1,100 µg per day, but European authorities set a lower limit of 600 µg per day.
The Wolff–Chaikoff effect is the thyroid's built-in brake, a temporary slowing of hormone production during surges of iodine intake. Most healthy people can adapt and return to normal, but in others, the brake fails or overcorrects. Excess iodine can trigger hypothyroidism, especially when coupled with autoimmune thyroiditis (Hashimoto's), or hyperthyroidism (the Jod-Basedow phenomenon), which is likelier in people with nodular goiter or long-standing iodine deficiency. Excess iodine can also trigger newborn thyroid problems when mothers take high-iodine supplements during pregnancy or breastfeeding.
Here's the problem with seaweed supplements:
1. They contain highly variable amounts of iodine. One gram of dried kombu, for example, can contain more than a thousand µg of iodine, and some samples contain several times that much. A small pinch of seaweed can contain more than an adult's upper limit for iodine intake for the day.
2. They're in powder and tablet form, making it easy to consume large amounts of dried seaweed unnoticed.
3. They can be taken in combination with a kelp capsule, a "thyroid support" supplement, an iodine-containing multivitamin, and iodized salt. The total amount of iodine consumed is never added up.
4. Products marketed for fatigue, weight loss, and "sluggish thyroid" will attract people most likely to have conditions that excess iodine worsens.
There are many case reports of thyroid dysfunction tied to kelp supplements and seaweed products, both in adults and in infants exposed to high iodine intake in utero or via breast milk. Be wary of products that don't state the iodine content per serving in micrograms.
But doesn't Japan eat seaweed?
Japan has one of the highest iodine intakes in the world, mostly from seaweed, and estimates of iodine intake there vary widely, from one to several milligrams (mg) per day, well above Western upper limits for iodine intake. But there's no thyroid crisis in Japan.
1. People have adapted to this iodine intake throughout their lifetimes. The thyroids of people exposed to iodine from childhood might regulate better than those that suddenly start receiving a concentrated iodine supplement.
2. People get their iodine from food, not pills. When seaweed is eaten as part of a meal, it's a varied amount and type of seaweed, and nori and wakame contain much less iodine than kombu.
3. It's prepared differently. Kombu is used to make dashi broth, which is then discarded or eaten in small amounts, and soaking and boiling seaweed removes a substantial share of the iodine, though some does end up in the broth.
4. It's consumed in a variable way. The intake varies day to day, not in a steady, high supplement-like dose.
Japan's record isn't spotless: iodine-related hypothyroidism has been documented in Japan, especially in heavy consumers of kombu, and clinicians often advise people with certain thyroid conditions to limit their seaweed intake.
Our tradition of high iodine intake shows that it can be tolerated in the right context. But it doesn't show that taking a concentrated kelp capsule is harmless for an adult who's been raised on a low-iodine diet.
(If you're not sure how much iodine you're getting from seaweed and other foods, I recommend you calculate your total daily iodine intake. See "What's Your Iodine Intake?" in the references.)

A financial bubble refers to a situation where an asset’s price rises far beyond what its underlying value justifies. Prices continue to climb on the expectation that they will continue to rise, rather than on the expectation of more earnings, income or usefulness. As the buying frenzy subsides and buyers run out of money to spend, confidence cracks, and prices fall fast – and that sudden fall is known as the “burst”.
The impact of financial bubbles is especially dangerous because debt magnifies losses. If prices fall, borrowers cannot repay their loans, lenders pull back from lending, and forced selling pushes prices lower. But money also flows into assets, lifting prices and encouraging more borrowing.
1. Market Bubbles
The impact of market bubbles is rarely contained. When home values fell during 2007 and 2008, banks, builders and insurers were hit, pulling the wider market down sharply. Stocks tied directly to the bubble often fall hardest, but even unrelated companies can be pulled lower as investors sell whatever they can.
5. Credit Bubbles
Defining example: The 2008 financial crisis, when bank stocks collapsed, credit froze and the S&P 500 fell more than 50% from its 2007 peak to its low in March 2009.
3. Stock Market Bubbles
The textbook example of a stock market bubble is the dot-com bubble of the late 1990s, when money poured into internet-related firms, many of which never had any profits, and sometimes barely had a business plan. The Nasdaq peaked in March 2000 and lost roughly three-quarters of its value over the next couple of years. Recoveries from these types of bubbles can take years, with the Nasdaq not regaining its 2000 peak until 2015.
4. Economic Bubbles
The classic case of an economic bubble is Japan in the late 1980s, when soaring stock and real estate prices made the country feel invincible, but both collapsed in the early 1990s, sending the economy into a state of stagnation that lasted for years. The Nikkei peaked at the end of 1989 and didn’t return to that level for more than 30 years.
3. Stock Market Bubbles
The danger for beginners is buying near the top of a bubble after a story becomes popular. No one can time a crash perfectly, and financial bubbles have a habit of inflating longer than seems rational, but patterns still tend to recur. When prices are far above underlying fundamentals – such as when valuations like price-to-earnings ratios are compared to historical averages and are found to be extremely high – it’s a sign that deserves skepticism.
When credit is easily available, with low lending standards, heavy borrowing and leverage, it can amplify the effects of a bubble.
When profits are weak or nonexistent, be wary of valuations that are based on promises rather than results.
If the main reason for buying a stock is that the price is rising, that’s a sign to pause.
How Can New Investors Protect Themselves?
Avoid leverage while you learn.
Keep an emergency fund to avoid forced selling in a downturn.

The brain immune response in neuronopathic Gaucher disease appears to make mouse brains more resistant to Sindbis virus. However, these findings are preliminary and apply to animals, not people.
A Quick Primer on Gaucher Disease
A faulty enzyme leads to an accumulation of lipids within cells. Types 2 and 3 of the disease are called neuronopathic, because glucocerebroside accumulates within nerve cells causing neurological damage.
The Interferon Connection
In neuronopathic Gaucher disease, the pathway seems to be on without infection. The buildup of lipids and cellular stress triggered a chronic low-level alarm. This switch on hundreds of genes stimulated by interferon, causing nearby cells to enter an “antiviral state.”
Normally, persistent inflammation is thought to drive neuronal damage and progression of the disease. However, this new study asks if the brain is primed with antiviral defenses, what happens when a real virus comes along?
To answer this question, researchers tested mice with Gaucher disease against Sindbis virus, a virus that infects neurons and causes encephalitis. This makes it a useful model for studying brain defense. The scientists compared Gaucher-model mice with controls and exposed them all to the virus.
Protection from Sindbis infection was linked to a pre-existing type I interferon response. Because the immune system was already active, the mice had a head start.
Why This Matters
Inflammation is a double-edged sword: neuroinflammation is often treated only as a problem to suppress, but the same processes can protect. Future therapies that target the interferon pathway in Gaucher disease will need to weigh both sides.
GBA variants are a significant genetic risk factor for Parkinson’s disease, with carrier rates elevated in some populations, including Ashkenazi Jews. Why do some disease variants stay common? The classic explanation is that one copy of the gene might give some advantage, such as how the best-known example is the sickle cell trait and protection against malaria. The authors call for research to find out whether Gaucher patients, and possibly GBA carriers, have some protection against certain viral infections. This is an open question, not a conclusion.
It’s important to note that the disease models used are not carriers: the mice were modeled to have full neuronopathic Gaucher disease. Carriers of Gaucher disease have far milder or no biochemical changes in their brain. Whether this priming of the immune system also occurs in these carriers is unknown.
And because the researchers tested only one virus, resistance to Sindbis does not imply resistance to others. In fact, some infections might be worsened by a chronically activated immune system.
The bottom line: future work in human cells and patient populations, as well as carriers of Gaucher disease, is needed.

Defenders of the traditional definition of marriage imagine a single, stable, and unchanging arrangement passed down from generation to generation. But the historical record is a little messier.
Marriage could exist without either a priest or a religious ceremony. It required the consent of the parties and their intention to live as husband and wife (the affectio maritalis), but not any particular ritual or sacrament. Divorce was comparatively easy, because marriage rested on the continuing consent of the parties, not on a sacred bond, and it ended when that consent ended. Romantic love was not expected to be a foundation of marriage; affection could grow, but love was a pleasant bonus, not a requirement.
The point is that the institution was never primarily about romantic fulfillment. For most of history, it was an economic and political technology.
In the 12th and 13th centuries, marriage was formally recognized as one of seven sacraments. In the Fourth Lateran Council of 1215, the rules were tightened, including a requirement for a public announcement of intended marriages in order to discourage secret unions and clarify who was married. Divorce became far harder, and marriage was fixed in Western law and culture as a lifelong union between one man and one woman. After the Reformation, Protestants rejected the sacramental nature of marriage but continued to see it as a divinely ordained institution, and civil governments inherited the Church’s definitions.
In the modern era, the Church’s grip on marriage began to loosen, as civil marriage statutes, secular courts, and no-fault divorce allowed marriage to be recast as a legal status run by the state. As the culture shifted to the idea that people should marry for love, the former side benefit of marriage became its central justification. This is crucial to the current debate: If marriage is defined as a loving, committed partnership between two adults, then limiting marriage to opposite-sex couples becomes a pressing question.
I find the caution argument to be the most respectable of the defenses of the traditional definition of marriage, but it is weakened by the fact that marriage has already been redefined repeatedly (by the end of arranged unions and no-fault divorce, for example). The procreative argument is that marriage unites the two kinds of people who can create children, and that it gives children a mother and a father. Of course, childless and infertile couples are permitted to marry without the legitimacy of their unions being questioned.
Finally, there is a religious argument that marriage is sacred, and that it is defined by a particular faith. To change it is to alter something that was never the state’s to change.
Those who favor allowing same-sex couples to marry cite the legal benefits that the state gives to married couples, such as inheritance rights, hospital visitation rights, tax treatment, parental rights, and immigration status. Denying some couples those benefits is unequal treatment, they argue, and marriage is a civil right. Most people already hold a love-based model of marriage: if adults marry for love and to share their lives, then the gender of their partners is irrelevant to the modern purpose of marriage. A society that celebrates marriage for love can hardly justify excluding people who love differently.

You walk into the exam, feeling ready after all those hours you spent with your notes. Within minutes, you can’t answer any of the questions. You recognize the material, but you can’t produce it. It’s not a failure of effort, but a failure of calibration—the match between how prepared you feel and how prepared you are.
When we reread material, it becomes familiar. Familiarity produces a sense of fluency, a feeling of ease in processing. Our brains mistake this fluency for mastery. But recognizing material and recalling it are different skills, and exams usually demand the latter. In a 2013 review, cognitive scientists John Dunlosky and colleagues rated both recognition and recall as having “low utility” when it comes to long-term learning. Highlighting a sentence with a yellow marker is a way of showing yourself you noticed it was important, not that you could explain it, apply it, or remember it next week.
In a 2008 study, cognitive scientists Jeffrey Karpicke and Henry Roediger found that people who repeatedly practiced self-testing, rather than rereading, remembered far more information a week later. The strategy accomplishes two jobs at once: strengthening memory and providing honest feedback. Take, for example, explaining the causes of World War I from memory. You get stuck after the second point, but now you see a gap in your knowledge, rather than waiting to find it out on test day.
Self-testing can take many forms: flashcards to be answered before flipping, blank-page “brain dumps,” practice problems without notes, and explaining a concept aloud to a friend.
But when instructors ask, “Does everyone understand?,” they fail because students who don’t understand often don’t know it. One way to get more honest feedback is to ask students to fill out short surveys before and after exams. Instructors can then use the results to see if certain study methods led to better outcomes. This technique—called “exam wrappers,” and developed by Marsha Lovett at Carnegie Mellon University—is a well-known version.
Students can reflect on how many hours they studied, what methods they used, and which topics they felt most and least confident about. They can predict their score and compare it to the actual score. The comparison is the point. If a student predicted a 90 and earned a 72, for example, there’s concrete evidence that their sense of preparedness was off. When students complete these surveys repeatedly over the course of a semester, they begin to learn which confidence feelings they can trust and which study habits paid off.
But even if students use these strategies, if they don’t actually do them, they won’t work. Self-testing is uncomfortable because it exposes what you don’t know. But that’s why it’s worth it. In the words of cognitive scientists Robert and Elizabeth Bjork, self-testing is a “desirable difficulty.” These are challenges that are harder in the moment, but produce stronger learning in the long run.
The simple rule is this: If a study method feels easy, be suspicious of it. The goal is not to feel ready for the exam, but to test whether you are, before the exam does it for you.
